lead: This unit shows how a circular shaft twists under torque, how to size it for strength and stiffness, and how to transmit power. It then covers shafts in series and parallel, combined bending and torsion, and helical and leaf springs. After it you can compute shear stress, angle of twist, power capacity and spring deflection.
about: The unit starts with the torsion formula for solid and hollow circular shafts, 6.1, and uses it to find shear stress at any radius. Chapter 6.2 adds angle of twist and separates strength from stiffness. Chapter 6.3 turns torque and speed into transmitted power. Chapter 6.4 extends the same formula to shafts in series, shafts in parallel and tapered shafts. Chapter 6.5 combines bending and torsion to find principal stresses and equivalent moments. Chapter 6.6 moves to helical springs, where axial load becomes torsion in the wire, and compares close-coiled and open-coiled behaviour. Chapter 6.7, taught by only a few universities, treats the leaf spring as a set of bending cantilevers.

chapters.idea: Torque on a circular shaft produces shear stress that is zero at the centre and maximum at the outer surface, and the torsional formula links torque, stress, radius and polar second moment of area.
chapters.depth: Cover the assumptions: circular sections stay circular, plane sections remain plane after twist, material is elastic and stress stays proportional to radius. Derive τ/r = T/J = Gθ/L; define τ (shear stress at radius r, Pa), T (torque, N·m), r (radial distance, m), J (polar second moment of area, m⁴), G (shear modulus, Pa), θ (angle of twist, rad), L (length, m). Give J = πd⁴/32 for a solid shaft and J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 for a hollow shaft, with D outer and d inner diameter. Draw stress distributions. Some syllabi call J the polar moment of inertia and the result the torsion equation.

figure.aria: Line graph: shear stress rises linearly from zero at the centre to maximum at the surface for a solid shaft; for a hollow shaft it starts at the inner radius.

chapters.example: A solid steel shaft of diameter 60 mm carries a torque of 2.5 kN·m. Find the maximum shear stress. T = 2500 N·m, d = 0.060 m, r = 0.030 m. J = πd⁴/32 = 1.272 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. τmax = T r / J = 2500 × 0.030 / (1.272 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.90 × 10⁷ Pa = 59.0 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using diameter in place of radius in τ = T r / J, or subtracting the inner diameter from the outer diameter instead of the fourth powers in J for a hollow shaft.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for shear stress and shear modulus; Unit 4 for second moment of area.
chapters.leave: Angle of twist to 6.2, power to 6.3, combined bending to 6.5.

chapters.idea: Angle of twist θ = TL/(GJ) measures deformation; a shaft is safe only if it passes both the strength limit on shear stress and the stiffness limit on twist per unit length.
chapters.depth: Cover θ = TL/(GJ) with θ in radians, T in N·m, L in m, G in Pa, J in m⁴; convert θ to degrees by multiplying 180/π. Define torsional rigidity GJ (N·m²) and torsional stiffness k = GJ/L (N·m per rad). State strength condition τmax ≤ τallow and stiffness condition θ/L ≤ qallow, where qallow is allowable twist per unit length (rad/m). Compare solid and hollow shafts of equal weight; hollow gives more torsional stiffness for the same mass. Include strain energy U = T²L/(2GJ) for a shaft in torsion, called torsional strain energy in some syllabi.

figure.title: Two checks on a shaft
figure.aria: Flowchart: torque gives shear stress for the strength check and twist for the stiffness check.

chapters.example: A solid steel shaft 50 mm diameter and 2.0 m long has G = 80 GPa and carries T = 1.2 kN·m. Find maximum shear stress and angle of twist. d = 0.050 m, r = 0.025 m, J = πd⁴/32 = 6.136 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴. τmax = T r/J = 1200 × 0.025/(6.136 × 10⁻⁷) = 4.89 × 10⁷ Pa = 48.9 MPa. θ = TL/(GJ) = 1200 × 2.0/(80 × 10⁹ × 6.136 × 10⁻⁷) = 0.0489 rad = 2.80°.
chapters.trap: Putting θ in degrees directly into θ = TL/(GJ), or mixing G in GPa with T in N·m without converting.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for the torsion formula and J.
chapters.leave: Power to 6.3, series and parallel to 6.4, combined loading to 6.5.

chapters.idea: A rotating shaft transmits power P = Tω = 2πNT/60, so torque falls as speed rises for the same power.
chapters.depth: Cover P = 2πNT/60, with P in watts, T in N·m, N in revolutions per minute (rpm). For P in kilowatts use P = 2πNT/60000. Define angular speed ω = 2πN/60 rad/s. Show the design route: given P and N find T, then use τmax = 16T/(πd³) for a solid shaft to find d, or J for a hollow shaft. Mention that a shaft may be limited by strength or by allowable twist; use 6.2 for the stiffness check. Some syllabi call this power transmission by circular shafts.

figure.aria: Curve: for a fixed power of 10 kW, torque falls as shaft speed rises.

chapters.example: An electric motor delivers 15 kW at 1440 rpm. The allowable shear stress in the shaft is 40 MPa. Find the minimum diameter of a solid shaft. ω = 2π × 1440/60 = 150.8 rad/s. T = P/ω = 15000/150.8 = 99.5 N·m. For a solid shaft τmax = 16T/(πd³), so d³ = 16 × 99.5/(π × 40 × 10⁶) = 1.27 × 10⁻⁵ m³. d = 0.0233 m = 23.3 mm. Choose a standard 25 mm shaft.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to convert rpm to rad/s, or using kW in place of W in P = Tω.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for τ = 16T/(πd³); 6.2 for the twist check.
chapters.leave: Gear and belt drives, if taught, belong with machine design; series and parallel shafts to 6.4.

chapters.idea: Shafts in series carry the same torque and add their twists; shafts in parallel share the torque in proportion to their torsional stiffness; a tapered shaft has constant torque but changing stress along its length.
chapters.depth: Cover series: θtotal = Σ TiLi/(GiJi) with the same T in every segment. Parallel: the same angle θ for each shaft, Ti = GiJiθ/Li, and Ttotal = ΣTi. Define torsional stiffness k = GJ/L and give 1/k = Σ1/ki for series and k = Σki for parallel. For a tapered circular shaft of length L with diameters d1 and d2, torque T is constant, J(x) = π[d(x)]⁴/32, and θ = ∫T dx/(GJ). For a linear taper, θ = 32TL/(3πG) × (d1² + d1d2 + d2²)/(d1³d2³); maximum shear stress occurs at the smaller diameter, τmax = 16T/(πdmin³). Some syllabi call this composite shafts or shafts in combination.

figure.title: Two shaft arrangements
figure.aria: Block diagram: in series the torque is common and twists add; in parallel the twist is common and torques add.

chapters.example: Two shafts are joined in series and carry T = 800 N·m. Shaft A: d = 50 mm, L = 1.0 m. Shaft B: d = 40 mm, L = 0.8 m. Both have G = 80 GPa. Find the total angle of twist. JA = π(0.050)⁴/32 = 6.136 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴; JB = π(0.040)⁴/32 = 2.513 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴. θA = 800 × 1.0/(80 × 10⁹ × 6.136 × 10⁻⁷) = 0.0163 rad. θB = 800 × 0.8/(80 × 10⁹ × 2.513 × 10⁻⁷) = 0.0318 rad. θtotal = 0.0481 rad = 2.76°.
chapters.trap: Adding torques in a series arrangement or adding angles in a parallel arrangement; using the same J for shafts of different diameter.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for J and τ; 6.2 for θ = TL/(GJ).
chapters.leave: Combined bending and torsion to 6.5; spring combinations to 6.6.

chapters.idea: When a shaft carries bending moment M and torque T together, the surface element has normal stress σ and shear stress τ; principal stresses and equivalent moments let you design the shaft.
chapters.depth: Cover σ = 32M/(πd³) and τ = 16T/(πd³) for a solid shaft, with M in N·m, T in N·m, d in m. For a hollow shaft replace d³ by D³(1 − k⁴) with k = d/D. Principal stresses: σ1,2 = σ/2 ± ½√(σ² + 4τ²); maximum shear stress τmax = ½√(σ² + 4τ²). Define equivalent bending moment Me = ½[M + √(M² + T²)] and equivalent torque Te = √(M² + T²). Design using d³ = 32Me/(πσallow) or d³ = 16Te/(πτallow). Some syllabi call this combined bending and torsion of shafts; the failure theories themselves belong to Unit 2.

figure.title: From M and T to a safe diameter
figure.aria: Flowchart: bending moment and torque give bending and shear stresses, then principal stress and equivalent torque, then shaft diameter.

chapters.example: A solid shaft of diameter 60 mm carries a bending moment M = 3.0 kN·m and a torque T = 2.0 kN·m. Find the maximum principal stress, maximum shear stress and equivalent torque. d = 0.060 m. σ = 32M/(πd³) = 32 × 3000/(π × 0.060³) = 1.415 × 10⁸ Pa = 141.5 MPa. τ = 16T/(πd³) = 16 × 2000/(π × 0.060³) = 4.716 × 10⁷ Pa = 47.2 MPa. σ1 = σ/2 + ½√(σ² + 4τ²) = 70.7 + 85.0 = 155.7 MPa. τmax = 85.0 MPa. Te = √(M² + T²) = √(3.0² + 2.0²) = 3.61 kN·m.
chapters.trap: Putting M and T straight into the principal stress formula without first converting them to σ and τ; dropping the factor 4 before τ²; using d instead of d³.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 and 6.2 for torsion; Unit 2 for principal stresses; Unit 4 for bending stress.
chapters.leave: Theories of failure and multi-axial design to Unit 2; columns to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A close-coiled helical spring mainly twists its wire under axial load, while an open-coiled spring also bends the wire because of the helix angle, so it is softer.
chapters.depth: Cover close-coiled assumptions: helix angle small, coil diameter much larger than wire diameter, axial load W (N) causes torsion T = WD/2 in the wire, where D is mean coil diameter (m) and d is wire diameter (m). Deflection δ = 8WD³n/(Gd⁴) with n active coils; stiffness k = W/δ = Gd⁴/(8D³n). Shear stress τ = 8WD/(πd³) ignoring direct shear; add direct shear as τmax = 8WD/(πd³)(1 + d/(2D)) or use Wahl factor where your syllabus asks. Strain energy U = ½Wδ. For springs in series 1/k = Σ1/ki; in parallel k = Σki. For open-coiled springs with helix angle α measured from the plane perpendicular to the axis, the wire carries torsion W R cos α and bending W R sin α; deflection is larger, δ = (8WD³n/(Gd⁴))[cos²α + (2G/E)sin²α] sec α. Some syllabi call these helical tension and compression springs.

figure.aria: Tree: close-coiled spring carries torsion only and deflects less; open-coiled spring carries torsion and bending and deflects more.

chapters.example: A close-coiled spring has mean coil diameter D = 50 mm, wire diameter d = 6 mm, n = 8 active coils, G = 80 GPa. It carries an axial load W = 200 N. Find deflection and maximum shear stress ignoring direct shear. δ = 8WD³n/(Gd⁴). D³ = 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ m³; d⁴ = 1.296 × 10⁻⁹ m⁴. δ = 8 × 200 × 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ × 8/(80 × 10⁹ × 1.296 × 10⁻⁹) = 0.0154 m = 15.4 mm. τ = 8WD/(πd³) = 8 × 200 × 0.050/(π × 2.16 × 10⁻⁷) = 1.18 × 10⁸ Pa = 118 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using coil diameter D in place of wire diameter d in d⁴, or counting total coils instead of active coils.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 and 6.2 for torsion and twist; Unit 1 for shear modulus and strain energy.
chapters.leave: Leaf springs to 6.7; spring surge and fatigue to machine design.

chapters.idea: A leaf spring is a set of graduated cantilever strips; the central load is shared among the leaves, giving a compact spring with bending stress spread along the length.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover the semi-elliptic leaf spring (also called laminated spring) with n leaves, width b, thickness t, length L between eyes and total central load W. Treat it as two cantilevers of length L/2, each carrying W/2. Then maximum bending moment M = WL/4 and maximum bending stress σ = 3WL/(2nbt²). Central deflection δ = WL³/(4nEbt³). Explain why the leaves are graduated: shorter leaves carry less moment, so the section modulus reduces towards the ends and the stress stays closer to uniform. Mention nipping and pre-stress in one line. Some syllabi use W for the load on one side and L for the cantilever length; use the symbols defined in your question.

figure.aria: Stack of leaf-spring strips: the master leaf is longest at the top and the other leaves become shorter towards the bottom.

chapters.example: A semi-elliptic leaf spring has total central load W = 6.0 kN, length L = 1.0 m between eyes, n = 8 leaves, width b = 60 mm, thickness t = 8 mm, E = 200 GPa. Find maximum bending stress and central deflection. σ = 3WL/(2nbt²) = 3 × 6000 × 1.0/(2 × 8 × 0.060 × 0.008²) = 2.93 × 10⁸ Pa = 293 MPa. δ = WL³/(4nEbt³) = 6000 × 1.0³/(4 × 8 × 200 × 10⁹ × 0.060 × 0.008³) = 0.0305 m = 30.5 mm.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that the load is shared by n leaves, or using the full length L as the cantilever length without halving the load.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 for simple bending of a cantilever; 6.6 for spring stiffness ideas.
chapters.leave: Helical spring design to 6.6; fatigue and spring materials to machine design.
